1. ACCESSIBILITY GATE:

NEVER guess study design or bias ratings from citation/title!

2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not applicable / not assessable — The study is a retrospective comparative institutional narrative synthesizing secondary sources rather than a prospective cohort, trial, or panel tracking individual units, though temporal coverage and reported metrics vary unevenly across the four country cases.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern — No empirical strategy isolates ownership structure from major concurrent historical confounders, including 1980s macroeconomic crises, European Union environmental quality standards in England and Wales, rapid urban demographic growth, hydrological scarcity versus abundance, and multilateral lending conditionality.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Weak — Key legal and institutional milestones (such as England and Wales's 1974 nationalization and 1989 privatization, Buenos Aires's 1993 concession and subsequent renegotiations, Côte d'Ivoire's SODECI lease/concession contracts, and Israel's 1959 Water Law) are described only via secondary academic/World Bank literature and ministry webpages, with zero citations to primary statutes, regulations, or concession texts.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern — Neither ownership/regulatory exposures nor water and sanitation performance outcomes are measured with standardized instruments; statistics are compiled uncritically from heterogeneous secondary reports, government webpages, and utility promotional material (such as Aguas Argentinas 2001).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak — Reported outcomes (network connection counts, coverage percentages, tariff changes, consumer surplus estimates, productivity, and informal vendor price/quality variability) are non-standardized across the four countries and rely on unverified secondary sources and utility self-reports.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: High concern — There is no pre-specified protocol, literature search strategy, or standardized cross-case outcome set; different outcomes and episodes are selectively emphasized in each country narrative depending on available secondary literature.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern — Both the four country cases (chosen specifically because they had already introduced privatization and possessed an extensive published literature) and the secondary sources cited within each case were purposively and non-systematically selected, excluding non-privatizing comparators or poorly documented failures.

domain_ratings.justification: Although the paper traces major statutory and contractual shifts (England and Wales's 1974 reorganization and 1989 privatization, Buenos Aires's 1992/1993 concession and 1994/1997 contract revisions plus mandatory connection/outlawing of shallow wells, Côte d'Ivoire's 1959/1967/1974/1988 SODECI contracts, and Israel's 1959 comprehensive water law), it cites zero primary statutes, regulatory instruments, or concession contracts, relying entirely on secondary academic papers, World Bank/UNDP reports, and government press/ministry webpages.

domain_ratings.justification: The case narratives generally distinguish subnational and contested jurisdictions well—such as Buenos Aires Federal District versus surrounding districts and provincial concessions in Córdoba and Buenos Aires province, Abidjan versus secondary Ivoirian cities, and pre-1948 Palestine, sovereign Israel, and Palestinian Authority areas (Gaza Strip and southern West Bank)—though the text occasionally conflates 'Britain' with 'England and Wales' when summarizing utility privatization.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Chenoweth (2004) presents a comparative historical-institutional four-country case study (England and Wales/Britain, Argentina, Côte d'Ivoire, and Israel/Palestinian territories) examining how public, privatized, and small-scale independent ownership structures in water supply and sanitation have evolved over time. Appraised under the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework as a structured non-validated judgment, the paper's chief strength lies in its rich contextual synthesis of institutional arrangements, contract structures, regulatory tensions, and the de facto role of informal/independent water providers alongside formal utilities (D10 strong; D2, D3, D5 adequate). However, methodological rigor for empirical or legal inference is weak overall: the paper contains no dedicated Methods section, relies entirely on secondary literature, utility self-reports (e.g., Aguas Argentinas 2001), and ministry webpages rather than primary statutes or concession contracts (D1, D7 weak), selects only countries that privatized and generated substantial published literature (D6, D11 weak), uses non-standardized outcomes across cases (D4 weak), and offers narrative chronology rather than credible causal identification or confounding control (D8, D9 weak).
raw_response.overall_rating: Weak overall methodological rigor (structured non-validated judgment: strong institutional context and adequate jurisdictional, exposure, and case-selection description, but weak primary legal sourcing, selection neutrality, measurement standardization, causal identification, and confounding control)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Comparative historical-institutional four-country case study based on secondary literature and official reports
raw_response.where_found_summary: Case selection rationale in Introduction (PDF p. 3 / p. 139); country institutional narratives in Development of Water Supply and Sanitation Sector covering England and Wales, Argentina, Côte d'Ivoire, and Israel (PDF pp. 3-8 / pp. 139-144); cross-case synthesis and GDP per capita comparisons in Discussion and Conclusion (PDF pp. 8-9 / pp. 144-145); source base in References (PDF pp. 10-11 / pp. 146-147). No standalone Methods section is present.
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The paper explicitly analyzes the historical-institutional evolution of water and sanitation ownership and regulatory regimes across four country case studies (Britain/England and Wales, Argentina, Côte d'Ivoire, and Israel) using secondary academic/policy literature, agency webpages, and macro statistics. It conducts no primary qualitative fieldwork such as interviews or ethnography (ruling out CASP), applies no systematic review search or screening protocol (ruling out AMSTAR 2), and implements no quantitative quasi-experimental comparator design (ruling out ROBINS-I), making the 13-domain Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework the appropriate instrument for a comparative institutional/legal-historical case study.
